Operator
Ladies and gentlemen, thank you for standing by. Welcome to Douglas Emmett's Quarterly Earnings Call. Today's call is being recorded. At this time, all participants are in a listen-only mode. After management's prepared remarks, you will receive instructions for participating in the question-and-answer session. I would now like to turn the conference over to Stuart McElhinney, Vice President of Investor Relations for Douglas Emmett. Please go ahead.
Stuart McElhinney
VP of Investor Relations, Douglas Emmett
Thank you. Joining us today on the call are Jordan Kaplan, our President and CEO, Kevin Crummy, our CIO, and Peter Seymour, our CFO. This call is being webcast live from our website and will be available for replay during the next 90 days. You can also find our earnings package at the investor relations section of our website. You can find reconciliations of non-GAAP financial measures discussed during today's call in the earnings package. During the course of this call, we will make forward-looking statements.
These forward-looking statements are based on the beliefs of, assumptions made by, and information currently available to us. Our actual results will be affected by known and unknown risks, trends, uncertainties, and factors that are beyond our control or ability to predict. Although we believe that our assumptions are reasonable, they are not guarantees of future performance, and some will prove to be incorrect.
Therefore, our actual future results can be expected to differ from our expectations, and those differences may be material. For a more detailed description of some potential risks, please refer to our SEC filings, which can be found in the investor relations section of our website. When we reach the question-and-answer portion, in consideration of others, please limit yourself to one question and one follow-up. I will now turn the call over to Jordan.
Jordan Kaplan
President and CEO, Douglas Emmett
Good morning, and thank you for joining us. The recent fires in and around Los Angeles have been devastating, impacting many of our friends, partners, and coworkers. Douglas Emmett is supporting the city's recovery efforts with our personnel and expertise. Fortunately, none of our properties were damaged by the fires. We've made significant progress on several key growth initiatives. In January, we purchased an office property and by-right residential development site at the corner of Wilshire and Westwood Boulevards.
In Burbank, following the move out of Warner Bros., we have begun redevelopment of our 456,000 sq ft Studio Plaza office building to convert it into a multi-tenant property. We are signing leases that will commence as common areas and the related floors are completed. Our 712-unit Barrington Plaza residential property now has a permit to begin construction.
As expected, our Q4 was adversely affected by the Warner Bros. departure. Lower office occupancy and higher interest rates also negatively impacted 2024 revenues and FFO. However, we maintained stable office rental rates, good control over our operating expenses, and continue to produce strong performance across our residential assets. Excluding the Warner Bros. move-out, we achieved positive absorption during H2 of 2024, even with muted Q4 leasing due to the holidays both falling midweek. Looking ahead, our 2025 lease expirations are 25% lower than 2024's record high and well below our 5-year average. We're also seeing a rebound in demand from larger office tenants. Given these factors, I'm optimistic that we will achieve positive absorption during 2025. I am also excited that our ongoing development projects will provide strong long-term growth.
Kevin can provide some details on our new development project.
Kevin Crummy
CIO, Douglas Emmett
Thanks, Jordan, and good morning, everyone. As Jordan mentioned, we formed a new joint venture to acquire a 17-story, 247,000 sq ft office building and adjoining residential development site in Westwood. We estimate the JV's total investment, including acquisition, upgrades to the existing tower, and construction of a new residential building, will be approximately $150 to 200 million over a 3- to 4-year period, depending upon our final plan. The new JV obtained a $61.8 million secured non-recourse interest-only loan that matures in January 2030 and has a fixed rate of 6% until July 2027 and 6.25% thereafter. We manage and own a 30% interest in the new JV and expect to enjoy significant operating and leasing synergies due to the proximity of our other Westwood properties.
During December 2024, we also closed a $325 million loan for another of our joint ventures in which we own 20%. The loan replaced a $400 million loan that we paid down using cash on hand in that JV. The new debt matures in December 2028 and is secured by five office properties, with interest swapped at a fixed rate of 6.36% until January 2028. With that, I will turn the call over to Stuart.
Stuart McElhinney
VP of Investor Relations, Douglas Emmett
Thanks, Kevin. Good morning, everyone. For all of 2024, we signed 876 office leases totaling a record 3.8 million sq ft for an average of 945,000 sq ft per quarter. During the Q4, we signed 204 office leases covering 796,000 sq ft, including 242,000 sq ft of new leases and 554,000 sq ft of renewal leases. New leasing demand from tenants over 10,000 sq ft improved again in Q4 and is now back to our pre-pandemic average. The overall value of new leases we signed in the quarter increased by 4%, with cash spreads down 7%.
At an average of only $5.46 per square foot per year, our leasing costs during Q4 remained well below the average for other office REITs in our benchmark group. Our residential portfolio remained essentially fully leased at 99.1% with good demand. With that, I'll turn the call over to Peter to discuss our results.
Peter Seymour
CFO, Douglas Emmett
Thanks, Stuart. Good morning, everyone. Reviewing our results compared to Q4 2023, revenue decreased by 5.5% due to lower office occupancy, which, combined with higher interest expense, lowered FFO to $0.38 per share and AFFO to $58.7 million. Same-property cash NOI decreased by 4.5% due to lower office revenues, partly offset by 6% multifamily growth and good expense control. At just under 5% of revenue, our G&A remains low relative to our benchmark group. Turning to guidance, we expect our 2025 net income per common share diluted to be between -$0.17 and -$0.11, and our FFO per fully diluted share to be between $1.42 and $1.48. Our guidance includes the consolidation of our previously unconsolidated fund and the new joint venture that we just formed.
However, we do not expect a significant contribution to FFO from the new joint venture during 2025, as we only own 30%, and we expect NOI to be impacted by construction. For information on assumptions underlying our guidance, please refer to the schedule in the earnings package. As usual, our guidance does not assume the impact of future property acquisitions or dispositions, common stock sales or repurchases, financings, property damage insurance recoveries, impairment charges, or other possible capital markets activities. I will now turn the call over to the operator so we can take your questions.
Operator
We will now begin the question-and-answer session. To ask a question, you may press star then one on your touch tone phone. If you are using a speakerphone, please pick up your handset before pressing the keys. If at any time your question has been addressed and you would like to withdraw your question, please press star then two. At this time, we will pause momentarily to assemble our roster. In consideration of other participants, we ask that you please limit your queries to one question and one follow-up. Thank you. Our first question comes from Alexander Goldfarb with Piper Sandler. Please go ahead.
Alexander Goldfarb
Managing Director and Senior Analyst, Piper Sandler
Hey, good morning. Morning out there, and certainly thoughts and prayers with those affected in the communities. Jordan, first question I'm sure you can imagine is, you know, we're reading a lot about, you know, some local politicians proposing, you know, or wanting to have rent freezes or eviction moratoriums. Just, you know, a sense of on the ground what you think, you know, the likelihood of any of these happening and, you know, how you think, you know, if CEQA and the Coastal Commission truly will stand down and allow the development to go on, or if you think they're also gonna be, you know, challenging some of the governor's emergency initiatives.
Jordan Kaplan
President and CEO, Douglas Emmett
In terms of the rent freezes, I mean, I hope they don't do anything. I know it was, like, moved kind of off the agenda for a while. It snuck back onto the agenda. I don't know what's gonna happen with it. I'm hopeful from conversations that we don't have to face that again. It certainly hasn't been good for the production of rental housing. In terms of the Coastal Commission.
CEQA impacting the redevelopment of the Palisades. If you're talking about the Palisades for Coastal Commission, for sure. I think the governor's order was extremely clear, and then he reissued a second order to make sure it was triply clear when the Coastal Commission came back and said, We still wanna be involved. In terms of kind of the politics and the way the Coastal Commission's created, if what he wants is them not to be involved, they're not gonna be involved. He came on super strong. By the way, the city also came on super strong. They wanna fast-track the reconstruction, and they're working pretty hard to make sure, in their words, in conversations I've had with them, to make sure they stay out of their own way. I'm optimistic on that front.
Alexander Goldfarb
Managing Director and Senior Analyst, Piper Sandler
Okay. Then the second question, Jordan, is you gave optimistic, you know, outlook that you'll see positive absorption this year and that leasing is trending the right way. But when we look at the occupancy for the year, the guidance is 78 to 80, which is basically, you know, I think we're 79 now. So how do we drive, you know, that average office occupancy, which basically applies flat with your positive comments on absorption and leasing trends?
Jordan Kaplan
President and CEO, Douglas Emmett
Well, I mean, office occupancy is a range, to be fair, but I will also say occupancy is people moving in. We're working on a lot of leasing. Leasing has a lag time, and especially if we're successful, and we get positive absorption out of the year. You've seen this, I know you've seen this in the past, that when our leasing amps up, the spread between leased and occupied widens. I'm hopeful that we see positive absorption on leasing, and of course, that's always like a great sign for occupancy moving up or eventually moving up. But there's a real lag there all the time.
Alexander Goldfarb
Managing Director and Senior Analyst, Piper Sandler
Thank you.
Jordan Kaplan
President and CEO, Douglas Emmett
All righty.
Operator
Our next question will come from Nick Yulico with Scotiabank. Please go ahead.
Nicholas Yulico
Analyst, Scotiabank
Thanks. You know, following up on the leasing topic and guidance, is there a way you could give us a feeling for, you know, leasing volume assumed in guidance this year, you know, versus last year, you know, flat, up, down, in order to get to, you know, the occupancy range that you're talking about?
Jordan Kaplan
President and CEO, Douglas Emmett
Last year, at the end of the year, we saw a real slowdown, which, you know, a leading indicator for us is showings. We saw it really slow down. I mean, real, you know, like below, you know, substantially below the amount of showings we would expect to have even in December because of the way that kind of those two Wednesdays with holidays, so people seemed to have sort of blown out both weeks at the end. But so it didn't even get to our average, and we're now seeing showings in January and going forward that are way above our average.
And that's one, if not, there's others of the reasons I'm just feeling, you know. It's that combined with that we have historically very low move-outs or very low roll this year. I should've said roll, not move-outs. We have very low roll this year, which we typically expect to get about 70% of. When you have lower roll, and then you turn around, and you go, I'm feeling good about showings, and you're feeling good about the pipeline, then I'm gonna be optimistic, and I'm telling you guys that I am.
Nicholas Yulico
Analyst, Scotiabank
Okay, thanks. I guess secondly is just in terms of you know if you could just talk about how a little bit more about how January leasing is shaping up. You know, I don't know how much January really makes or breaks a year or not, but anything you could talk about in terms of you know if the fire has impacted you know whether it's sort of existing tenants thinking about space or you know leasing decisions that were you know kind of in the works with people if there's you know been any impact so far on leasing.
Jordan Kaplan
President and CEO, Douglas Emmett
I think it's very hard to tell whether the fire is gonna have any impact on it. Quite frankly, I don't think it is. I, you know, there's not any data out there to figure that out yet. Even if it does have a tiny impact, and I couldn't even tell you if it would be plus or minus, the tide, the general positive tide that I just described, in terms of kind of our outlook and what's going on, I think would overwhelm it. I don't think it would be meaningful anyway.
Nicholas Yulico
Analyst, Scotiabank
All right. Thanks. Appreciate it.
Jordan Kaplan
President and CEO, Douglas Emmett
All right.
Operator
Our next question will come from Steve Sakwa with Evercore ISI. Please go ahead.
Steve Sakwa
Managing Director and Senior Analyst, Evercore ISI
Yeah. Thanks. Good morning. Jordan, I know you're probably loathe to talk about like cap rates on individual deals, but can you just help us kind of size up maybe what the economics look like for both kind of the office and the planned apartment at the new acquisition of 10900, just so we can kind of help think about either stabilized yields, IRRs. You know, how do we think about that investment?
Jordan Kaplan
President and CEO, Douglas Emmett
That's great that you know. I mean, we've only been working together for, what? This is almost our 20th year or something. That's true. I hate cap rates. I don't think cap rates are particularly indicative other than a cap rate on a, like, at market leased apartment building. But I will, because you asked, I will say with you knowing, I really don't like cap rates as an indicator of anything, that I think we're going in at a little over a 10 cap rate, and I expect when we're done with all our work to be over 10 cap rate.
Steve Sakwa
Managing Director and Senior Analyst, Evercore ISI
Just to be clear, that's just on the office component, or that's office and residential combined?
Jordan Kaplan
President and CEO, Douglas Emmett
Well, going in couldn't be on anything but the office. Coming out, it's combined.
Steve Sakwa
Managing Director and Senior Analyst, Evercore ISI
Okay. Moving up to the Warner Bros. building, just as we think about the money you're putting in, the $75 to 100 million of you know CapEx redevelopment. You know, I know Warner Bros. was paying kind of low 60s rent on that building. When you're done with the work, how do you think the new rents for the multi-tenant building will stack up to that prior rent?
Jordan Kaplan
President and CEO, Douglas Emmett
I think that. Well, I will say this. Remember, they just moved out, like, a month or two ago. I think that we're very pleased with our leasing, and you know, we're not talking about individual deals, but we try to describe in our prepared remarks that, you know, we're already leasing. What's now is, like, we got to get this work done and get the common areas done and get some of these floors done so we can get these people in and paying. I would say this, we feel very good about what's going on there.
Steve Sakwa
Managing Director and Senior Analyst, Evercore ISI
Okay, thanks.
Jordan Kaplan
President and CEO, Douglas Emmett
Okay. Thanks, Dan.
Operator
Our next question will come from Blaine Heck with Wells Fargo. Please go ahead.
Blaine Heck
Senior Office and Industrial REIT Analyst, Wells Fargo
Great. Thanks. Good morning out there. Just to follow up on a couple of your answers, can you remind us what the lag is between leasing and occupancy that's typical in your portfolio? I guess you mentioned 70% for retention. Just to confirm that's what you guys are expecting this year, especially given that we noticed you've got a lot of expirations in the valley towards the end of the year. Are those a concern at all?
Jordan Kaplan
President and CEO, Douglas Emmett
We are expecting, and I got to tell you historically, with a lot of regularity of experience, I think the real number is like 69-point something, and that's very reliable historically. Quarter to quarter, it's not a big deal, but it's very reliable over, you know, 3, 4 quarters. That's why we're expecting, and then I would expect it here. That was your question on renewal. What was your other question?
Blaine Heck
Senior Office and Industrial REIT Analyst, Wells Fargo
Just the typical lag between leasing and occupancy.
Jordan Kaplan
President and CEO, Douglas Emmett
That number can range from 100 to, like, 350 basis points and even higher. I mean, if you're really leasing at a torrid pace, it gets up above 300. When things are extremely lackluster, it can get down to 100. I would say if you just look at it like a, you know, there's never a normal time in real estate. Anything you would call a normal time may be 150 basis points. I got to tell you, if you go back a few years when we were doing a ton of leasing, Greg, I don't know if you remember going back, but there was a time when like sort of COVID was over, but I know people weren't talking about recessions.
We had a kind of a weird year there where we got positive again. I remember we got up to about 350, and everyone was saying, When are they gonna move in? When are they gonna move in? I said, Well, you just wanna keep that 350 because it means we're just doing a lot of leasing. 'Cause they were trying to, like, get the 350 back down. You don't want it to go down 'cause, you know, those people move in, you wanna have more people that are in that pipeline. That seems to be the nature of it.
Stuart McElhinney
VP of Investor Relations, Douglas Emmett
Blaine, if you're asking about timing on moving folks in after we've signed a lease, typically it's, you know, very quickly. We can move folks in in the quarter or within two quarters of when they sign their lease. Of course, on Studio Plaza with building out multi-tenant quarters and that kind of stuff, it's gonna take longer.
Jordan Kaplan
President and CEO, Douglas Emmett
Yeah.
Blaine Heck
Senior Office and Industrial REIT Analyst, Wells Fargo
Great. Very helpful.
Jordan Kaplan
President and CEO, Douglas Emmett
Good question.
Blaine Heck
Senior Office and Industrial REIT Analyst, Wells Fargo
No, it's fine. That was helpful commentary from you too, Jordan. Just secondly on the acquisition, you know, it looks like this is a new JV partner. If that's the case, can you tell us anything about that partner and their willingness to do more deals with you? Whether GIC was considered as a partner and kind of their ongoing interest in investing with you. Thanks.
Jordan Kaplan
President and CEO, Douglas Emmett
We don't really like to talk about our JV partners, and to be perfectly frank, they're not anxious to be in the press. If they wanna say something themselves, they're always welcome to do it. But, you know, we've been asked the question, I got to tell you, I think every quarter for now 4 or 5 years, we've been asked whether our JV partners still had an interest in buying office, still had an interest in resi, had a this, that, and the other, and I said, yeah they definitely do. You can look at the fact of how much we got squeezed down on this deal to know how aggressively they do wanna be in these deals. I mean, that money is out there.
I'm happy that we were able to do a deal and give those guys some way to have some participation, 'cause if you don't give them deals, you're gonna lose their attention. I know, like, Kevin's been doing a good amount of traveling with Stewart and Griff, and they've been getting out and continuing saying to those guys, we think we're gonna be able to make deals, and now we're making them. I'm super happy about that.
Blaine Heck
Senior Office and Industrial REIT Analyst, Wells Fargo
Thank you.
Operator
Our next question will come from Jeff Spector with Bank of America. Please go ahead.
Jeff Spector
Managing Director and Head of United States REITs, Bank of America
Great. Thank you. Jordan, follow-up question on your comments around absorption. You know, when we've met you in the past, you've talked about, you know, I guess if there's, you know, healthy positive absorption, you wanna see one-third new, you wanna see two to four, 10- to 15,000-square-foot tenants. Can you know, provide a bit more color on what you're seeing in the market that backs up your thoughts for 25, besides the fact that you have less roll? Thank you.
Jordan Kaplan
President and CEO, Douglas Emmett
Less roll makes a big difference, that for sure. But we're just getting a lot of activity, as Stuart has said, and you know. This is one of the questions he was gonna answer, but we again saw last quarter a great return of the over 10,000-square-foot tenants and back to like at or above our norm, which has been what's been missing in terms of us achieving really the big goal, which is to get something in the 800,000s and to be one-third new. We were really having trouble getting there with the one-third new because we need some of these larger guys to come back, and they've come back.
Add on to that, as this year has launched out, I mean, we're just feeling much better about everything that's going on in terms of the actual lease activity, the showings, and all the rest of it. I mean, that's what caused me to write that in our prepared remarks.
Jeff Spector
Managing Director and Head of United States REITs, Bank of America
Thank you. I guess, could you talk a little bit more about that new demand, in particular, the larger tenants, what type of industries they're coming from or they're in, I should say? Thank you.
Stuart McElhinney
VP of Investor Relations, Douglas Emmett
Yeah. We saw demand across the board. You know, it wasn't concentrated in any particular industry. We saw real estate, we saw across the board kind of demand in Q4 for those larger tenants.
Jeff Spector
Managing Director and Head of United States REITs, Bank of America
Thank you.
Operator
Next question will come from Michael Griffin with Citi. Please go ahead.
Michael Griffin
Analyst, Citi
Great. Thanks. Maybe to expand a little bit on Jeff's question surrounding the large tenant demand. I mean, in your summation, you know, what has maybe changed in that, you know, tenants' mindset that makes them more confident to go out and sign leases? Is it improved business confidence? Is it an updated outlook on the economy? I know that work from home was never really an issue with your tenant base, but maybe just kind of the why you're seeing those sort of tenants come back to the market.
Jordan Kaplan
President and CEO, Douglas Emmett
You know, I didn't know why they weren't back last year. I didn't really know that many large tenants were taking sort of a posture to prepare to be in a like extreme recession or that's what's coming or whatever. I'm sure that attitude has changed, and that's played some role. I got to tell you, I also watched our leasing group, our operating platform, and I will add our kind of development group, which we kind of maintained and actually oddly grew during this time, and a lot of people are kind of falling away from some of those things. They've adjusted strategies. You know, they've figured out how to be and where to be aggressive in this market and how to get attention.
I don't know whether it's us, it's everybody, it's them changing their attitude, but we are some of it is just I can see it in our platform because I saw when we were bidding against that other deal that was going on, and other people that were trying to come in the market because they might have thought that would be a good deal. I could see that we're now substantially more qualified to handle and take advantage of these opportunities, both from leasing perspective in terms of even our platform's even more robust now, and from the perspective of having not only maintained but sort of built up our development platform. I mean, this is rare. We're now taking on multiple development deals.
I know on that deal we've just bid on, I don't think anyone was even realizing there was another development opportunity there. I'm feeling really good about all. I mean, I feel great about it, not even just really good about our growth stuff. I wrote that in my prepared remarks. Like, we have a lot of growth things going on now.
Michael Griffin
Analyst, Citi
No, that's a helpful color. I can definitely, you know, gauge the excitement in your voice there. Then, you know, just maybe one follow-up on the 10900 Wilshire acquisition. You know, do you envision this as a big tenant building? You know, would it be more your bread-and-butter kind of tenants? And anything you can comment on, you know, the upcoming rent roll or lease maturities, and whether or not there's a mark-to-market opportunity in the building.
Jordan Kaplan
President and CEO, Douglas Emmett
That building uniquely has presented us with more than one extremely good option, and before we talk more about it, we need to decide what direction we're going in. We need to spend a little more time on that. I feel that that building provides a lot of opportunity, but we got to decide what direction we're gonna go in, and we need to get that done relatively soon. I'm gonna let that sit for a while.
Michael Griffin
Analyst, Citi
Sounds good. Appreciate it. That's it for me.
Operator
The next question will come from Richard Anderson with Wedbush. Please go ahead.
Richard Anderson
Managing Director, Equity Research, Wedbush Securities
Thanks. Good morning. A quarter or two ago, Jordan, you had mentioned, you know, on Studio Plaza, I hope it's not single tenant, and now it's definitely not single tenant, it sounds like, based on the money you're spending. What have you guys done to sort of gauge the market to get you to the point where you're, you know, so committed to multi-tenant execution that you're spending that kind of money on it? Was there some work done on the ground to say, Okay, we got some, you know, real opportunity here, but it's not gonna be 450,000 sq ft? I'm just curious what the process was.
Jordan Kaplan
President and CEO, Douglas Emmett
I think you're talking about Studio Plaza, which is-
Richard Anderson
Managing Director, Equity Research, Wedbush Securities
Excuse me. Excuse me.
Jordan Kaplan
President and CEO, Douglas Emmett
The old tenant was Warner Bros.
Richard Anderson
Managing Director, Equity Research, Wedbush Securities
Yeah, yeah.
Jordan Kaplan
President and CEO, Douglas Emmett
Warner Bros.
Richard Anderson
Managing Director, Equity Research, Wedbush Securities
You know what I meant.
Jordan Kaplan
President and CEO, Douglas Emmett
It would've been. Look, I'm not gonna say just like all good developers and leasing guys, I mean, if we would've had the problem of we're turning down a 450,000 foot tenant, I guess maybe I don't know that we would've turned that down. I had never seen us do that. I'm not sure that we had really the options the way you're describing it. I will say that we like that market a lot. Our comfort level is not with large tenants. We like the distributed risk of multi-tenant buildings. It's a great market. We did benefit from it being a single-tenant building, or well, we had a decade in there when it wasn't.
In general, two out of the three decades, it was a single-tenant building. I'm pleased now. Obviously nobody likes having their building vacant, but I'm pleased that we have an opportunity now to extremely de-risk that building and lease it up. Like I said, we like what we're seeing on the lease-up. I mean, we like what's going on, so that's good.
Richard Anderson
Managing Director, Equity Research, Wedbush Securities
Do you think you'll have some real concrete stuff to talk about in the quarter that quickly from a leasing perspective?
Jordan Kaplan
President and CEO, Douglas Emmett
Well, I'm really telling you we're signing leases.
Richard Anderson
Managing Director, Equity Research, Wedbush Securities
I mean, actual numbers.
Jordan Kaplan
President and CEO, Douglas Emmett
If you're saying to me, are we gonna start, like, tracking it that way? No. We're not gonna, you know, just take one building and start tracking it. If you're asking me in terms of, like, having the building ready for those tenants to move in, we have actually given a bunch of info on that, and that work's going on. I think we might even have some imagery and stuff on our website on that building, and you could see what it's gonna look like going forward as has been seen by the people we're leasing to and to our prospects.
Richard Anderson
Managing Director, Equity Research, Wedbush Securities
Okay. Second question, interest expense is projected to be up 15% or so year-over-year. A lot of, you know, clear rationale behind that, swap expirations and so on. I'm wondering if the environment is causing you to sort of change your way, I mean, your approach to the balance sheet at any level. You know, you're kind of exposed to quite a bit of variable rate debt and that increases as time passes in 2025. Anything you can share with how you might, you know, manage this situation in the current macro environment?
Jordan Kaplan
President and CEO, Douglas Emmett
Well, we've never been in love with variable rate debt. It's just that you got to go variable when a loan's coming up, right? We normally borrow 7 years and fix it for 5, and we expect to refinance. Because of the way the market's been, we've been stuck with stuff that's kind of during those 2 years has gone to floating. It's not that that's been a strategy. As you can see from the deals that we did, which Kevin described in his prepared remarks, those deals are fixed, right? They're both in the sixes. I mean, we're willing to live with that.
As stuff comes up and we have the opportunity to make those changes with a longer-term loan and those opportunities, then we're probably gonna swap it or do fixed rate deals.
Richard Anderson
Managing Director, Equity Research, Wedbush Securities
Okay, good enough. Thanks very much.
Jordan Kaplan
President and CEO, Douglas Emmett
All right.
Operator
Next question will come from Anthony Paolone with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.
Anthony Paolone
Executive Director, JPMorgan
Thanks. You know, maybe we'll stay on debt for a minute. If we look out to 2026, I think you have about $1.3 billion coming due. Any likelihood of addressing some of that earlier than next year, and is any of that in guidance? Also, just anything we should be looking out for as we look out to that, whether it's a big increase in spreads or where some of that debt might reside at the asset level that we need to consider?
Jordan Kaplan
President and CEO, Douglas Emmett
Well, we just announced two deals, so you have some comps on interest rates, right? In terms of working on them, we definitely wanna deal with them this year and are working on that. Because of the way the market is, it's as equally uncomfortable for us as everybody that we're having to walk down the line so far and deal with these loans when they're so much closer to maturity. The '26 debt, we at this time are very focused on dealing with now and making deals and extending out, and we're definitely working on that.
Anthony Paolone
Executive Director, JPMorgan
That there's some of that in the interest rate guidance, I assume.
Jordan Kaplan
President and CEO, Douglas Emmett
No, because we don't include in our guidance deals that aren't done. When those deals are done, then that'll go in there. Until they're done, we don't include like prospective or potential deals in the guidance.
Anthony Paolone
Executive Director, JPMorgan
Got it. Okay. Just a follow-up, you know, on 10900, you talked about, you know, how much you like the deal and it's pretty unique. Should we think about that as one-off, or, are you seeing, capital markets thaw out there and a deal pipeline starting to build more broadly?
Jordan Kaplan
President and CEO, Douglas Emmett
Do you wanna answer?
Kevin Crummy
CIO, Douglas Emmett
Sure. This is Kevin Anthony. We did see a number of larger tenant format buildings that traded last year, but that's not what we do. We're looking for multi-tenant assets that we can apply our operating platform to. This was a great opportunity. It was a perfect fit. You know, I'm optimistic that there's gonna be more of that in our markets over the coming year.
Anthony Paolone
Executive Director, JPMorgan
Okay, thanks.
Operator
The next question will come from John Kim with BMO Capital Markets. Please go ahead.
John Kim
Managing Director, BMO Capital Markets
Thank you. I could see why you wanted to disclose the 10% cap rate on 10-900. But I wanted to ask about that. On the office side, I think, Jordan, you mentioned that's the going-in cap rate, but you do have some options. I was wondering if there was some maturities and maybe some upside of that 10% if you redevelop it. Then on the multifamily, developing at a 10% yield, is that an affordable housing multifamily development, and that's the reason why you can get that attractive yield? Just wanted some more details, if you could provide it.
Jordan Kaplan
President and CEO, Douglas Emmett
I said above 10%. I didn't say 10%, just to be clear, in both instances. The multifamily is not low income. It's that market.
John Kim
Managing Director, BMO Capital Markets
How were you able to get that in? It's hard to develop above a six, I think, in multifamily.
Jordan Kaplan
President and CEO, Douglas Emmett
I mean, it's a function of our, you know, everything surrounding the deal. It's rents in the area. It's the cost to build a building. It's the price we paid and how that option was included in the deal. I said it on an earlier, you know. Oh, Kevin's reminding me by writing on a piece of paper that it does not include. There's no allocation of land because I'm telling you right now we bought it with no building, and I just gave you the cap rate. You're assuming that we're building it for a 10 cap rate. Anyways, in what I told you is for the entire project. It's not just for the apartment building.
Not to say that it won't be a high cap rate, but it's what I described earlier about kind of people's recognition of that opportunity with respect to this deal. I'm pretty sure we're the only ones that saw it because we have such a kind of robust development platform to begin with, and we know what's going on here, obviously. You know there's been some changes to state law that we're very familiar with. I've been pointing out to you guys that there's locations along Wilshire that we own today and that now, like it's a new world. Now you can by-right build resi.
You know, with all that knowledge here and our development group and being able to understand costs and the fact that literally, you know, I don't know, blocks away in Brentwood, we just built a high-rise. We just have a lot of information on this front. We were able to recognize the opportunity and be able to also add that in. There's, you know, it's very easy to do. We paid a price that I think when we're bidding against everybody just contemplated that it was the building that's standing there today.
John Kim
Managing Director, BMO Capital Markets
Congrats. It sounds great. Just wanted to follow up on your guidance. What is contemplated as far as capitalized interest, and how did capitalized interest end up last year? I think you were on an $8 million run rate in 2024.
Peter Seymour
CFO, Douglas Emmett
Yeah. It's Peter. I mean, we don't give guidance specifically on capitalized interest. You know, you can assume that as we expand development, there'll be a bit more of it. Yeah, I think that's all I have to say on that.
John Kim
Managing Director, BMO Capital Markets
Can you remind us if Studio Plaza has secured that?
Peter Seymour
CFO, Douglas Emmett
It does not.
John Kim
Managing Director, BMO Capital Markets
Great. Thank you.
Operator
The next question will come from Dylan Burzinski with Green Street. Please go ahead.
Dylan Burzinski
Analyst, Green Street
Good afternoon, guys. Thanks for taking the question. Jordan, just wanted to go back to your previous comment about having existing density within the operating portfolio today. I know you guys kind of alluded to it in the past, but can you kind of describe just how big of an opportunity set that is?
Jordan Kaplan
President and CEO, Douglas Emmett
Have I told people that in the past?
Kevin Crummy
CIO, Douglas Emmett
It's thousands of units.
Jordan Kaplan
President and CEO, Douglas Emmett
Okay. It's thousands of units.
Dylan Burzinski
Analyst, Green Street
I guess, I mean, is there any sense for a lot of these to be near-term endeavors, or are these sort of longer-term in nature in terms of being able to actually get at that and start development process?
Jordan Kaplan
President and CEO, Douglas Emmett
I've been asked in the past, like, how rapidly are we going because there was changes in state law and whatnot, how rapidly are we gonna move in and continue building units 'cause we're a primary owner along Wilshire, where most of this is impacted by the exchanges. I had said in the past, you know, I think our goal would be to do a deal in Hawaii and a deal in LA. You know, have two deals going at a time, at any particular time, but the deals take a few years, and then you finish them, and then you go to the next thing.
You would say, Well, wait a minute, you're already in, like, more than 1 deal here, because we're doing Barrington complete redo, and now we also just took on another one. As I said, I mean, I think it's a function of how strong our development group has become, and maybe it is the case that we could take on more than 1. But I'm not anxious to take on many more than 2. We have 2 now, and it just takes a lot. We have 3 now? Do we have 3 now? Yeah. Okay, we have 3 now. Stuart's putting fingers up 3. Yeah, we have a lot going on.
Dylan Burzinski
Analyst, Green Street
Great. One more, if I may. You mentioned tenant activity over 10,000sq ft getting back to sort of pre-pandemic levels. Can you kind of just talk about, you know, what you guys think is sort of driving this renewed optimism amongst this cohort of tenants?
Jordan Kaplan
President and CEO, Douglas Emmett
Well, I think there's two kind of big things going on. Number one is, I do believe larger tenants are doing a bit of an about face, and they're no longer in a completely guarded position vis-à-vis like a dramatic recession that's gonna come and beat the place up. I think that shift is definitely making a difference. I'm gonna tell you, I also see a difference in our penetration in the market and our teasing out tenants and getting access to tenants and getting these deals made. It's hard for me. I don't know how to separate the two, but I could tell you we got a lot more big tenant deals going. We got a lot of people focused on it. I mean, if you ask any...
You know, we have 800 people, and if you go to any of them and go, What's going on? They'll go some, but they're gonna go, Leasing, leasing. I mean, that's what's been going on. So if you say that long enough, hard enough, focused enough, and are, you know, strategic enough, you're gonna do leasing, and you know. So that's what's happening.
Dylan Burzinski
Analyst, Green Street
Great. Appreciate your comments.
Operator
Question comes from Upal Rana with KeyBanc Capital Markets. Please go ahead.
Upal Rana
Senior Analyst, KeyBanc Capital Markets
Great. Thanks for taking my question. The $335 million loan that matures in March and that you're currently in the process of negotiating an amendment and an extension on, what have the conversations been like, and what's the probability of the amendment finalizing by the due date?
Jordan Kaplan
President and CEO, Douglas Emmett
I mean, I don't think I'm prepared to discuss that, anything that's going on there right now. I mean, obviously, you've already outlined what's going on, and that's probably the amount we're willing to discuss. We don't like to discuss deals, certainly in process, and we really actually announce them after they're gone and closed.
Upal Rana
Senior Analyst, KeyBanc Capital Markets
Okay, sure. My other question would be on the 10900 acquisition. You have about 40,000 sq ft expiring this summer with some of it being sublet as well. What's your confidence that those tenants may re-sign? Have you had any preliminary conversation with those tenants prior to purchasing the asset, especially with your plans to upgrade the existing tower?
Jordan Kaplan
President and CEO, Douglas Emmett
Well, I mean, we're in the market. We're obviously familiar with all the tenants, so you know, I don't know that I can. I mean, we're not gonna talk about individual tenants. We kind of gave you, we have a couple paths we can follow, and we have to decide what path we're going to follow. I don't wanna give guidance on a building like for midterm. We kind of gave you where we are today and where we're confident we're headed. It has a lot going on. It has redevelopment, it has the residential. It has a lot going on. We need to just play that out and make some better decisions about it, or make some decisions about it. I'm sure it'll be good.
Upal Rana
Senior Analyst, KeyBanc Capital Markets
Okay. Thank you.
Operator
Our next question will come from Jamie Feldman with Wells Fargo. Please go ahead.
Jamie Feldman
Managing Director and Head of REIT Research, Wells Fargo
Great. Thanks for taking the question. You know, just thinking big picture about the impact of the wildfires. You know, if you fast-forward a couple of years here, you know, what do you think is gonna be most different about Los Angeles, going forward? You know, based on the conversations going on with rebuilding and planning, you know, what are you most optimistic about, and what causes you the most concern about things moving forward?
Jordan Kaplan
President and CEO, Douglas Emmett
This morning, there was an article in The New York Times about the Palisades, and it made a lot of projections about where the Palisades is headed in terms of a market, in terms of the people that are gonna be there, and how the Palisades is gonna change and the focus it's getting. I read it, and I thought that that outcome was. That was probably as good a guess as anything, because there's a lot of history around other communities that have been impacted by fire, which is devastating. I mean, I didn't spend a lot of time at the beginning of this thing, but you can't imagine how much time. Personally, the people here at Douglas Emmett, I personally can. I mean, Stuart, Kevin, Peter's, you know, not even back in his house.
I mean, what's going on now is, I would have never imagined. If you wanna, like, jump very far forward and say, like, where does this all go in the end? You look at what has happened in Malibu and other markets where fires come through. You already know that the city's dedicated to making a bunch of extremely positive changes to that area in terms of where, you know, supportive of development, allowing development to be more rapid. I know a lot of people are talking about lot combining. I know very few people are just saying, I'm out of here. Actually, almost to a T, people are either like, how fast can I rebuild, and they're also in the market for their neighbor's lot.
I see that happening, and I think to myself, this has been horrible destruction. We're gonna go through a rough few years, but it does give me optimism about where the Palisades is headed, and so we'll see.
Jamie Feldman
Managing Director and Head of REIT Research, Wells Fargo
Okay. Thank you for that. I know it's a difficult topic. I guess just thinking about commercial real estate, you know, we've heard about some high school leases in Santa Monica. Anything you think changes in terms of the demand profile for the different submarkets you're in or other submarkets that might be more interesting for you guys going forward, as you know, with the rebuild and changes?
Jordan Kaplan
President and CEO, Douglas Emmett
Well, I know we're talking to some schools too. I know there's some schools that have, like, kind of looked for space because of course they want to stay open, right? I mean, they have all the kids and that whole thing. I know that other schools that are, you know, were not damaged around Santa Monica. I'm on the board of one school in Culver City. I don't wanna mention them, but I know they're now accommodating other schools, students, and programs to try and help out. I know that is all going on.
Putting that aside, I have to say again, you know, the actual Pacific Palisades area, you know, they had one or two medical office buildings, medical with a little bit of normal office or some other normal office. There are the schools and there are businesses. But I'm not sure that transplant in the size of our market is going to be the thing that like makes a big difference. As I said, the tide of just the kind of tide of leasing, I think would overwhelm any of that. I know that I was asked earlier. I said like a lot of people just have been displaced and they're renting houses that might not be as big as their other, where they were before.
Work from home, to the small degree that it existed, might be much more difficult now. People want, you know, come in the office, maybe they're renting a smaller place. They don't have an office or something until they build their house back. I don't even think work from home was impacting us that much, so I'm not even. I can't even say that I think that will make a big difference to leasing and especially against where I think the tide of leasing is going.
Jamie Feldman
Managing Director and Head of REIT Research, Wells Fargo
Okay. I would assume Santa Monica get-
Jordan Kaplan
President and CEO, Douglas Emmett
Sorry, I don't know how to answer it.
Jamie Feldman
Managing Director and Head of REIT Research, Wells Fargo
No, that's super helpful. I mean, I would assume Santa Monica's would get the benefit from, you know, reconstruction type, you know, architects, engineers. I mean, is that the closest-
Jordan Kaplan
President and CEO, Douglas Emmett
Yeah, I think Santa Monica, Brentwood, and Westwood, all these areas here, I think that it's way too early for that to happen. If you're saying to me there's a lot of capital that's about to come into this place, and when more capital comes in, that means they need more office space, and there's gonna be construction and activity here in a big way for quite a few years. Yeah. I mean, that will incrementally, I'm sure, make a difference, but the difference hasn't had a chance to get made yet, so we aren't seeing it yet.
Jamie Feldman
Managing Director and Head of REIT Research, Wells Fargo
Okay. All right. Thank you. We send our best to your entire team.
Jordan Kaplan
President and CEO, Douglas Emmett
Thanks.
Operator
Our next question is a follow-up from Nicholas Yulico with Scotiabank. Please go ahead.
Nicholas Yulico
Analyst, Scotiabank
Thanks. Just going back to 10900 Wilshire, not to beat a dead horse on this, but it looks to us that you bought the leasehold in that asset. You don't own the ground. So is that correct? And is that also why the, you know, the cap rate yield expectation you're citing is, you know, higher than what some would expect?
Jordan Kaplan
President and CEO, Douglas Emmett
No, we bought it in fee.
Nicholas Yulico
Analyst, Scotiabank
Okay. Thank you.
Jordan Kaplan
President and CEO, Douglas Emmett
We own the ground and the building. We own both. We own the whole thing.
Steve Sakwa
Managing Director and Senior Analyst, Evercore ISI
Thank you.
Jordan Kaplan
President and CEO, Douglas Emmett
All righty.
Operator
This concludes our question and answer session. I would like to turn the conference back over to Jordan Kaplan for any closing remarks.
Jordan Kaplan
President and CEO, Douglas Emmett
Okay. Well, thank you for joining us. I know this was a complicated release, and I appreciate that you guys spent the time to look it over and had a lot of good questions, and we will be speaking with you again in a quarter. Goodbye.
Operator
The conference is now concluded. Thank you for attending today's presentation. You may now disconnect.

content.text:
Stuart McElhinney
VP of Investor Relations, Douglas Emmett
Thank you. Joining us today on the call are Jordan Kaplan, our President and CEO, Kevin Crummy, our CIO, and Peter Seymour, our CFO. This call is being webcast live from our website and will be available for replay during the next 90 days. You can also find our earnings package at the investor relations section of our website. You can find reconciliations of non-GAAP financial measures discussed during today's call in the earnings package. During the course of this call, we will make forward-looking statements.
These forward-looking statements are based on the beliefs of, assumptions made by, and information currently available to us. Our actual results will be affected by known and unknown risks, trends, uncertainties, and factors that are beyond our control or ability to predict. Although we believe that our assumptions are reasonable, they are not guarantees of future performance, and some will prove to be incorrect. Therefore, our actual future results can be expected to differ from our expectations, and those differences may be material.
For a more detailed description of some potential risks, please refer to our SEC filings, which can be found in the investor relations section of our website. When we reach the question and answer portion, in consideration of others, please limit yourself to one question and one follow-up. I will now turn the call over to Jordan.
Jordan Kaplan
President and CEO, Douglas Emmett
Good morning, and thank you for joining us. In 2023, higher interest rates fueled recession fears. As a result, tenants became more cautious, office leasing slowed, and our leasing gains immediately following the pandemic were reversed. Our office occupancy declined, but large fixed rent increases, stable rental rates, and low concessions in our markets mitigated the impact on revenue. Interestingly, remote work does not seem to have meaningfully reduced demand from our tenants. In addition, due to our typical five-year lease terms, more than two-thirds of our current leases were actually signed after the pandemic began.
As Peter will tell you, our 2024 guidance anticipates lower FFO as a result of vacating the Barrington Plaza Apartments, the expiration of one large lease, and higher interest costs. Our guidance does not take into account any significant recovery in leasing demand, even though we see the potential for that as tenant confidence increases. I am pleased that shortly after quarter end, one of our largest tenants signed an early renewal for 250,000 sq ft. We continue to grow our residential portfolio.
We have added almost 1,300 apartments over the last five years in our strongest markets. Despite removing Barrington Plaza from the market, our residential portfolio now provides almost 20% of our rental revenue. In addition, we have not experienced the residential building boom seen in other major markets, so our apartments remain fully leased. That said, the rapid rent growth during the pandemic seems to be normalizing. There are challenges and opportunities ahead. We are prepared for both as I am confident in the long-term prospects of our markets.
Our supply-demand dynamic is among the best in the US. Our sub-markets are vibrant, and our office tenants have overwhelmingly returned to work. We have significant cash on hand, meaningful free cash flow, no corporate level debt, and almost half our office properties remain unencumbered. With that, I will turn the call over to Kevin.
Kevin Crummy
Chief Investment Officer, Douglas Emmett
Thanks, Jordan, and good morning, everyone. I would just like to take a moment to mention that we have completed the lease-up of our 376-unit Landmark LA property in Brentwood. At our office to residential conversion in Honolulu, we finished the conversion of another office floor, and as expected, the 22 new apartments are leasing quickly. As the remaining two office floors vacate over the next few years, we will add the final 47 units to complete that project. Otherwise, our cash and strong JV relationships position us to take advantage of new opportunities in our markets, and we're focused on finding those opportunities in both residential and office. Stuart?
Stuart McElhinney
VP of Investor Relations, Douglas Emmett
Thanks, Kevin. Good morning, everyone. For all of 2023, we signed 872 office leases totaling 3.2 million sq ft for an average of 800,000 sq ft per quarter. During Q4, we signed 202 office leases covering 710,000 sq ft, including 243,000 sq ft of new leases and 467,000 sq ft of renewal leases. These results do not include the 250,000 sq ft renewal in Beverly Hills, signed after quarter end, extending the term for 10 years through 2037. The overall value of new leases we signed in the quarter increased by 4.3%. Cash spreads were down 6.1%, reflecting the strong annual rent increases built into our leases.
At an average of only $5.86 per sq ft per year, our leasing costs during Q4 remained well below the average for other office REITs in our benchmark group. Our residential properties continued to perform well during Q4, ending the year at 98.5% leased. With that, I'll turn the call over to Peter to discuss our results.
Peter Abramowitz
Equity Research Analyst and SVP, Jefferies
Thanks, Stuart. Good morning, everyone. Reviewing our results compared to Q4 of 2022, revenue increased by 2%, partly from higher multifamily revenues and ground rent. During Q4, we prevailed in a ground rent reset arbitration on land that we own. The result was a one-time payment of accumulated back rent of approximately $5.5 million, and going forward, there will be approximately $1 million of additional annual rent. FFO decreased by 12% to $0.46 per share, primarily as a result of higher interest expense.
AFFO decreased 8.1% to $74.6 million, and same property cash NOI decreased by 1.1%, driven by comparison to a strong prior period that benefited from one-time tax refunds on a residential portfolio. Adjusting for those items, residential cash same property NOI would've been +3.3%, and overall cash NOI growth would've been -0.6%. Our G&A remains very low relative to our benchmark group at only 5.6% of revenue. Turning to guidance, for 2024, we expect FFO per share to be between $1.64 and $1.70, reflecting the expected move out of one large tenant in Burbank, the removal of Barrington Plaza from the rental market, higher interest costs, and modest leasing assumptions.
For information on assumptions underlying our guidance, please refer to the schedule in the earnings package. As usual, our guidance does not assume the impact of future acquisitions, dispositions, or financings. I will now turn the call over to the operator, so we can take your questions.
Operator
We will now begin the question and answer session. To ask a question, you may press star, then one on your telephone keypad. If you are using a speakerphone, please pick up your handset before pressing the keys. If at any time your question has been addressed and you would like to withdraw your question, please press star then two. Again, in consideration of other participants, please limit your queries to one question and one follow-up. Thank you. At this time, we will pause momentarily to assemble our roster.
The first question comes from Blaine Heck with Wells Fargo. Please go ahead.
Blaine Heck
Senior Real Estate Equity Analyst, Wells Fargo Securities
Great. Thanks. Jordan, it seems like, some of the rhetoric in the market has shifted back towards interest rates that could be higher for longer. I guess, how are you thinking about where rates go in the next year or two? Has anything changed around your thoughts on kinda how to handle the upcoming swap and debt maturities in 2024 and beyond?
Jordan Kaplan
President and CEO, Douglas Emmett
The reason there's swaps coming up is that, you know, we typically do a seven-year loan, and we swap five years of it. That gives us a two-year window to then refinance the loan. Most of the time when swaps are coming up, it means that we need to, you know, start to have, I mean, a point of view toward refinancing. More importantly, it means that it's probably not worthwhile to try and swap two years or one year or whatever's left, which is to some degree what you see coming up.
As we refinance those loans, we'll focus on then, you know, swapping them, and they'll be fixed at whatever rate, you know, we're, you know, is in the market at that time, and hopefully we have a good spread.
Blaine Heck
Senior Real Estate Equity Analyst, Wells Fargo Securities
All right, great. That's helpful. Then just second question. With respect to Barrington Plaza, I guess, can you guys give any update on your expectation with respect to insurance proceeds, any update on litigation from prior tenants? Talk about kind of the mechanics of that project, especially how capitalized interest might impact numbers and just at a high level, how we should be thinking about kind of the impact to earnings this year and beyond.
Jordan Kaplan
President and CEO, Douglas Emmett
Okay, I'll answer the first part and I'll let Peter answer the second part. Well, go ahead, you can answer your section, then you can come back and ask me whatever you don't answer. Go ahead.
Peter Abramowitz
Equity Research Analyst and SVP, Jefferies
Yeah. Okay. It's Peter. Yeah, I mean, with respect to, you know, the impact of Barrington this year, we had about $0.045 of Barrington in 2023. You know, that will be reduced to about $0.005 in our numbers for 2024, mostly due to the remaining retail commercial tenants who are in the property. You know, our interest guidance, you know, assumes a certain level of capitalized interest. You know, obviously, that's gonna depend on how quickly we move and how much we spend.
Jordan Kaplan
President and CEO, Douglas Emmett
Okay. Your questions then revolved around the litigation and the insurance, right? Your beginning questions.
Blaine Heck
Senior Real Estate Equity Analyst, Wells Fargo Securities
Yeah.
Jordan Kaplan
President and CEO, Douglas Emmett
Well, we feel it's insured. I mean, we still have to get the insurers on board with that, so we're dealing with that. In terms of litigation coming from tenants, I mean, obviously, that is also insured, but, you know, it's ongoing and all, and all litigation is disruptive. I mean, that's a drag that it's going on, but, you know, we're dealing with that.
Blaine Heck
Senior Real Estate Equity Analyst, Wells Fargo Securities
All right, we'll stay tuned for an update. Thanks, guys.
Jordan Kaplan
President and CEO, Douglas Emmett
All righty.
Operator
The next question comes from Michael Griffin with Citi. Please go ahead.
Michael Griffin
Senior Equity Research Analyst, Citi
Great. Thanks. Jordan, I wanna go back to your comment you made on the leasing front. You know, you said that two-thirds of your leases have already been signed during or after the pandemic. Is it fair to assume that leasing is going to materially pick up in the next couple of years, or is this just kind of the new normal that we should expect?
Jordan Kaplan
President and CEO, Douglas Emmett
I fully believe that leasing will pick up over the next couple of years. As a matter of fact, I've tried to really make this point a huge amount of times, which is that you saw our leasing pick up right after the COVID kinda got lifted. What's happened now is the country and particularly a lot of people holding office space have gotten some sort of recessionary fear, shrinking, and cost-cutting. I mean, you don't hear about many companies saying, "Here's the units that we're expanding," right?
Everybody's focused on cutting expenses, and we're just, you know, one of the results from that going on across the country and certainly here. People aren't making big commitments to doing new things. Our smaller tenants are going forward great. You see it, you see we're doing a lot of leasing. Large ones are very hesitant around commitments. Frankly, what I keep seeing, and having nothing to do with COVID or return to work or any of it, I just see that they're showing, telling the analysts, you guys, what you wanna hear, which is we're cutting costs by cutting staffing, and there's just one article or another like that.
As soon as that lightens up, I fully expect the market to return to where we were before. By the way, most of our history when we weren't in a process of buying or acquiring a lot of vacancy, we have been at very high levels of occupancy with the portfolio ranging from, you know, 92 to 95, 96. You know, you go, "Well, what’s the reason for that? And why do we feel it’s such a great market?" Is what I said, we have the best supply-demand dynamic of any market in the United States.
We effectively have no new supply coming in, and we have a lot of industries that drive demand. I know, you know, nobody wants to keep hearing about tech and entertainment, but we have medicine, we have universities, we have research. All of those are our space takers. You're seeing articles about it, even today. I'm very optimistic about where our buildings will be headed as soon as what. You know, I think what you'll actually see is you'll see interest rates lighten up and tenants kind of come back strong into the market all around the same time. I mean, but we all need to make predictions about that, and I don't think they're market-specific for us.
Michael Griffin
Senior Equity Research Analyst, Citi
Gotcha. Appreciate the insights there. I was wondering if you could give some additional color on the 20% acquisition in your JV fund. Was this more opportunistic, given the existing relationship you have there, or should we read into this as you're looking more proactively at acquisition opportunities?
Jordan Kaplan
President and CEO, Douglas Emmett
In general, when we're in these JVs, our recommendation is always, you know, we think this is a good hold or we think we should all be selling at the same time. Then in the specific, when one of our JV partners wants to sell, we work hard to make sure there's a market for that and they can get liquidity. This is a, you know, this was a relatively small deal. I mean, it's not very material, but we were certainly happy to provide that liquidity for that partner that wanted to get out, and that's all that really happened there.
Michael Griffin
Senior Equity Research Analyst, Citi
Great. Well, that's it for me. Thanks for the time.
Jordan Kaplan
President and CEO, Douglas Emmett
All right. Thanks.
Operator
The next question comes from Nicholas Yulico with Scotiabank. Please go ahead.
Nicholas Yulico
Managing Director, Scotiabank
Thanks. Maybe first question is on, you know, acquisition opportunities and how you're thinking about, you know, those and particularly in relation to, you know, if you have a portfolio right now where you're already dealing with some unstabilized occupancy levels. I mean, are you still willing to go out and, you know, find investments if they pencil and make sense and put capital to work with JV partners?
Jordan Kaplan
President and CEO, Douglas Emmett
Absolutely. I mean, I think, I mean, we're definitely spending time trying to find deals, and I think it's an amazing opportunity right now. When I think back to the last time I thought it was such an obvious and amazing opportunity, which maybe the rest of the world didn't think, but it did turn out to be the case, you've got to go all the way back to 1990, 1991, 1992, 1993, when Ken and I were just getting going with this company, with Dan and Chris, and we looked at what was going on out there and we said, "Wow, I mean, the price you can buy these buildings for, assuming some of this stuff comes up and we have a chance to get it, they're epic.
Apparently, they're 130 years. I don't wanna miss that opportunity at all.
Nicholas Yulico
Managing Director, Scotiabank
All right. Thanks. Second is just on the William Morris extension. Are you able to give us any feel for how the rent spread worked on that? I mean, I guess we'll learn next quarter when you put the new rent in the sup, but any preview you can give us on that, along with how to think about, you know, the capital you had to extend to get the lease done?
Jordan Kaplan
President and CEO, Douglas Emmett
